tier_reason: The ch-bench README table (ClickHouse org, written by the ch-go author) lists clickhouse-cpp 516ms vs curl 3.7s, clickhouse-jdbc 7.2s, Python clickhouse-driver 37s and clickhouse-go 46.8s with public programs (ch-bench-cpp/bench.cpp, curl/run.sh, Makefile), but no CPU model, no compiler or C++ build flags and no server version are stated, and the table reports best results gathered across runs, so it cannot reach A; not an independent suite, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: ch-bench README table (best results, runs from January to June 2022): clickhouse-cpp 516ms / 6.9M RAM vs curl (C, HTTP) 3.7s, clickhouse-jdbc (Java, HTTP) 7.2s, clickhouse-driver (Python) 37s, ClickHouse/clickhouse-go (Go) 46.8s; the page's own ratio column gives clickhouse-cpp 1.47x, curl 9x, clickhouse-jdbc 18x, clickhouse-driver Python 106x, clickhouse-go 117x relative to the ~1x leaders (about 7.2x vs curl, 14x vs clickhouse-jdbc, 72x vs Python clickhouse-driver, 91x vs clickhouse-go, derived from page data). The repo's hyperfine exports give smaller Go gaps: RESULTS.md clickhouse-cpp 611.3 ms vs clickhouse-go 6529.0 ms (about 10.7x) and RESULTS.slow.md 579.5 ms vs 38253.9 ms (about 66x) (derived from page data). Not the fastest client: ch-go 401ms and the C++ clickhouse-client 387ms are faster, and the README's C++ hyperfine table puts clickhouse-cpp at 574.4 ms vs clickhouse-client 561.9 ms (parity).
corrections.caveats: Evidence lives in the separate ClickHouse/ch-bench repo (Apache-2.0, 36 stars, last commit 2023-08-31; README results table last edited June 2022, its C++ section January 2022), whose README calls it 'Totally unscientific and mostly unrealistic' and says the ClickHouse/ch-go project uses it to understand its own performance. The README table reports best results (not means) assembled from runs made months apart on unstated hardware, so every row reflects 2022-era client versions, and the repo's own hyperfine exports disagree on the Go rows (clickhouse-go 6529.0 ms in RESULTS.md and 38253.9 ms in RESULTS.slow.md vs 46.8s in the README). One synthetic query on localhost; CPU model, compiler and C++ build flags are not stated (the Makefile builds only the Go and Rust programs, Rust with -C target-cpu=native; ch-bench-cpp/bench.cpp has no build line) and the ClickHouse server version is not stated. The C++ program only sums block row counts (the library still decodes the UInt64 column); the curl row (curl/run.sh) pipes RowBinaryWithNamesAndTypes over HTTP to /dev/null under \time -v rather than hyperfine, so it measures HTTP transport and server-side row formatting with no client deserialization. The wins are native binary protocol vs HTTP and vs row-oriented or reflection-based Go/Java/Python clients; against the official C++ clickhouse-client (the natural C++ incumbent) and ch-go it is at parity or slower. Off-baseline for columnar-analytics: it is a client of ClickHouse compared with other ClickHouse clients, not faster than any listed engine. The repo's own bench/bench.cpp (Google Benchmark, SelectNumber over 1000 rows of three columns) has no baseline.

notes: Numbers match the ch-bench README exactly; tier C stands. Shortcomings to record: off-baseline (client-vs-client comparison, not faster than ClickHouse/clickhouse-client; parity with clickhouse-client in the C++ hyperfine table), stale 2022 best-of numbers mixed across runs, curl row timed differently and without client deserialization, no CPU/compiler/flags; baseline_in_list set to false because none of the compared clients is a category baseline.

tier_reason: performance-report.md (nightly, generated 2026-10-06, commit 3e4ff81) compares DoltLite with a stock SQLite reference built by test/build_stock_reference.sh, using public harness code (test/sysbench_compare*.sh, test/lib/sysbench_benchmark.sh, test/sysbench_timer.c, .github/workflows/nightly-performance.yml), but the runner is a shared ubuntu-latest GitHub runner with no CPU model and no compiler version, and the library builds use configure defaults, so first-party C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: No overall speedup claimed; the report is a regression gate with slowdown ceilings and DoltLite is slower on every aggregate (time, SQLite then DoltLite): in-memory reads 9.57s vs 11.12s (1.2x), in-memory writes 1.94s vs 3.03s (1.6x), file-backed reads 10.16s vs 11.24s (1.1x), file-backed writes 3.66s vs 4.03s (1.1x), autocommit writes 816.91ms vs 2.35s (2.9x). Individual integer-key file-backed rows where DoltLite is faster: oltp_point_select 64.75ms vs 30.79ms (0.5x time), select_random_ranges 7.90ms vs 4.29ms (0.5x), oltp_read_only 126.32ms vs 81.03ms (0.6x), oltp_write_only 80.38ms vs 59.68ms (0.7x). These read wins exist only against SQLite in its default rollback-journal mode: the ac_reads section runs the same SQL files with SQLite in WAL mode and the same rows become ties or losses (oltp_point_select 30.19ms vs 30.89ms, select_random_ranges 4.27ms vs 4.29ms, oltp_read_only 77.16ms vs 80.98ms).
corrections.caveats: Not a speed claim: the project's own docs (doc/doltlite/performance.md) say the stock comparison tracks 'the remaining SQL performance gap', and the nightly gate allows DoltLite to be up to 2.3x slower per workload (5.5x for autocommit writes). The file-backed rows where DoltLite wins are an artifact of the baseline configuration: in file_reads/file_writes stock SQLite runs with only PRAGMA cache_size=16384 in its default rollback-journal mode, and every read workload issues thousands of standalone SELECTs (10,000 for oltp_point_select), each its own read transaction; the ac_reads section runs the identical SQL files with SQLite in WAL mode (synchronous=FULL), where SQLite's point-select time halves (64.75ms to 30.19ms) and DoltLite ties or loses on every row. The same pattern holds in the textpk, blobpk and compositepk tables, and file-backed oltp_write_only is 1.2x and 1.3x slower for blob and composite keys. Shared GitHub-hosted runner (ubuntu24 20260927.320.1) with no CPU model; the timer harness is built with cc -O2 -Werror, the libraries with configure defaults, compiler version unstated. test/build_stock_reference.sh notes that CI once shipped a 'stock' reference that shared DoltLite's storage and so passed by construction; the current report uses the rebuilt, asserted stock reference, but older nightly numbers and blog figures may predate that fix (not verified). DoltHub blog posts (dolthub.com blocked; search snippets only) put the prolly-tree tax at 1.20x on reads, 1.67x on batched writes and 4.00x on autocommit writes, with file-backed reads about 5% faster to parity. Licence: DoltLite extensions Apache-2.0, inherited SQLite sources public domain (no patent grant for those). The README describes the project as the product of agentic engineering.

notes: All quoted numbers match performance-report.md, but the record presented per-row wins without noting that they vanish when stock SQLite uses WAL (the report's own ac_reads section, same SQL files); claim corrected, tier stays C. Record as shortcomings: not faster than SQLite (1.1x-2.9x slower on every aggregate), per-row wins only against default rollback-journal SQLite, shared CI runner without CPU model.
